Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: A nearby 10-story mid-rise Charles Schwab Corporation office building had minor exterior damage and a few broken windows.
A T.G.I. Friday's location in the Highland Plaza shopping district sustained collapse of its roof and exterior walls, and at least 8 people had to be rescued from that location.
A dentist's office sustained major structural damage.
A Chipotle, a Whataburger, and an AT&T store had their roofs ripped off.
Damage to ten of the affected businesses in the Highland Plaza district was so severe that city management designated them to be condemned.
Just past this area, the tornado struck the 18-story Remington Tower office building along Skelly Drive. The tower sustained major damage to its facade and exterior, and had many windows blown out.
A nearby hotel was also damaged.
An industrial building along East 42nd Street sustained EF2 damage, losing its roof and large portions of its masonry exterior walls.

Beyond this point, the tornado weakened to EF1 intensity as it moved through industrial areas, causing minor to moderate damage to warehouses and industrial buildings, with roofing and paneling removed and portions of exterior walls blown out.
The EF1 tornado crossed South Mingo Road into another industrial area, where several industrial buildings were damaged.

Crossing U.S. Route 64 and following East 51st Street South, the tornado produced EF1 damage as a motel and an industrial building sustained damage before dissipating near the intersection of East 51st Street South and South 145th East Avenue.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: At 7:14 p.m. (0014 UTC), it struck Northpoint as an EF2, causing severe damage to several homes. Roofs were removed entirely from homes, though the walls on these structures remained mostly intact.

The tornado entered Faulkner County and struck the River Plantation subdivision at the southwest edge of Mayflower. EF4 damage took place with large, two‐story homes being leveled with only piles of debris left on their foundations.
Just outside the subdivision, a power substation sustained major damage.

A recreational vehicle dealership on the other side of the highway was completely destroyed at EF4 intensity (with meteorologist Tim Marshall noting an EF3 rating due to structural flaws), along with most of the RVs; three were found wrapped around a nearby billboard.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Num: vehicle repair shop, millwork company, construction company, and church destroyed; home improvement store badly damaged
Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: In southern Mayflower, a vehicle repair shop, millwork company, construction company, and church were destroyed, and a home improvement store was badly damaged.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Num: Vilonia Middle School damaged and multiple downtown structures destroyed
Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Shortly before 7:50 p.m., the tornado moved into Vilonia at high‐end EF4 strength. It first struck the recently built Vilonia Middle School—destroying its top floor—and then completely destroyed a dollar store, a strip mall, two auto repair shops, the old city hall, a gas station, a church life center, a real estate office, an investment firm, an auto parts store, and a fried fish restaurant in downtown Vilonia. Additionally, a 29,998‐pound fertilizer tank was found displaced.
Shortly after 8:00 p.m. (0100 UTC), the tornado entered White County just west of El Paso, briefly regaining EF2 status and destroying two manufactured homes.

In addition to the storm shelter fatality, two other people were killed in Mayflower.
Nine people were killed in Vilonia.
One person was killed in one of the manufactured homes near El Paso.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: The tornado re-intensified as it continued sharply northeastward into the south side of Louisville at EF3 strength, destroying numerous homes in residential areas.

The tornado then passed through a wooded area and across the east edge of town, striking the Winston County Medical Center in the process. The building sustained EF3 damage, with numerous cars flipped and tossed in the parking lot.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: A daycare center and an automobile showroom were completely leveled across the street from the medical center, both of which were housed in manufactured structures.

The tornado made another sharp turn and began moving due-north through residential areas on the northeast side of town. Numerous homes sustained EF3 to EF4-strength damage in this area, including one that was reduced to a bare foundation slab.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Off the coast of Rakhine State, a large boat was towing two smaller ones to a safer area, late on May 13, when one or more of them capsized after striking rocks. By the following day, 42 people had been rescued and 8 bodies had been found.

In Arakan State, just outside Sittwe, 393 people were evacuated from low-lying areas.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: It then crossed Interstate 24 at Spring Street and produced major EF3‐strength damage in East Nashville, crossing the path of the April 16, 1998, F3 tornado in the Five Points neighborhood. Numerous businesses, restaurants, bars, homes, and apartment buildings were damaged or destroyed in Five Points, including Basement East (a popular music venue), a YMCA was badly damaged, and a Dollar General store was completely destroyed.

The tornado moved through Mount Juliet, producing a large swath of high‐end EF3 damage as it crossed North Mount Juliet Road and substantially damaged Mount Juliet Christian Academy, West Wilson Middle School, and Stoner Creek Elementary. Numerous homes throughout town were heavily damaged or destroyed, with some completely leveled.

In Lebanon, many homes and businesses suffered considerable damage, including two large cemeteries, Lebanon Municipal Airport, Walmart, and Lowe's, as the tornado crossed South Hartmann Drive, South Maple Street, and South Cumberland Street (U.S. 231). As it passed Linwood Road, a gas station and a heavy equipment auctioneer's property sustained low‐end EF2 damage.

Continuing into Smith County, the tornado produced EF1‐type damage in the Grant and New Middleton communities by snapping and uprooting trees, damaging or destroying barns and outbuildings, and causing considerable roof damage to homes. As it passed through southern Gordonsville (notably along Agee Branch Road, Hickman Highway, and Maple Street), further structural damages were observed before the tornado lifted.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: A strong F2 tornado hit the countryside just north of Viterbo. This tornado damaged many well-built farm houses, some of which sustained significant damage. Outbuildings were destroyed, and sheet metal was wrapped around trees and power lines. Many trees were snapped or uprooted, some of which sustained low-end debarking. A large metal electric pylon was blown over, a concrete power pole was snapped, and farming equipment was thrown and destroyed. Signs and fences were downed, and an animal breeding facility sustained roof loss and major damage to its brick exterior walls. Multiple animals were crushed by debris at this location.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: The outbreak started that morning when a large tornadic waterspout struck the eastern portions of the Italian city of Salerno, uprooting trees, causing light structural damage, and injuring one person.
That afternoon, a low‐end IF2/F2/T4 tornado struck and damaged two schools in Albertslund, Denmark.
In the same event, the tornado caused considerable damage to homes and trees along a 4.4 kilometer long path in Albertslund, Denmark.
One of the tornadoes from a couple of supercells in northern Italy remained over open fields and caused no damage in the Negrar area.
The other tornado in the supercell outbreak, in the Arba area, caused light damage to homes, trees, and anti-hail nets.
That evening, a waterspout made landfall in the Rosignano Marittimo area; the stronger of the two ripped roofs off structures, downed trees, and injured eight people.
A second waterspout in Rosignano Marittimo moved a few boats, lightly damaged a roof, and downed a few trees.
During the nighttime hours, a waterspout made landfall in northern France causing some light damage.
A second waterspout came ashore in eastern Genoa, causing some scattered damage.
On September 27 in Nettuno, trees were downed or damaged, a cemetery suffered some damage, roofs and sheet metal structures were severely damaged, and roulottes, campers, and cars were flipped.
On September 27, the Casal de Principe tornado downed trees and power poles, and caused damage to signs, small buildings, and roofs.
A small tornado struck Viriat, France and damaged some trees and greenhouses.
A large, strong F2 tornado touched down in Ukraine's Kherson region in the village of Velikaya Aleksandrovka, causing widespread damage to over 300 residential buildings.
The same tornado also caused damage to hundreds of other structures, including unroofing a school and damaging exterior walls, with many trees snapped or denuded.

Time_Annotation: A tropical disturbance developed on December 15 in the central Indian Ocean west of Diego Garcia, and the storm was last tracked by the MFR on December 28.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Bondo passed through the Farquhar Group of islands belonging to the Seychelles (and caused severe damage on Providence Atoll), and in Madagascar, Bondo killed 11 people when it struck the island's west coast.
Main_Event_Annotation: It strengthened into Moderate Tropical Storm Bondo on December 18 and rapidly intensified into tropical cyclone status, or the equivalent of a minimal hurricane.
Hazards_Annotation: The MFR estimated peak winds of 205 km/h on December 20 and the storm’s high winds (up to 155 km/h in Mahajanga) damaged buildings, while high waves caused flooding, particularly in the Seychelles archipelago.

Time_Annotation: Cyclone Favio developed as a tropical disturbance on February 11 to the southwest of Diego Garcia. The MFR discontinued advisories on February 23 when the storm was near the Mozambique/Zimbabwe border.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: In Mozambique, Favio killed 10 people and caused additional deadly flooding. The storm brushed the southern coast of Madagascar, and Favio dropped heavy rainfall across southern Africa causing flooding in eastern Botswana, Lesotho, Malawi, Tanzania, and Zimbabwe.
Main_Event_Annotation: The system was upgraded to Moderate Tropical Storm Favio, then to tropical cyclone status on February 19, and later intensified into an intense tropical cyclone.
Hazards_Annotation: On Rodrigues, the cyclone produced 114 km/h wind gusts and heavy rainfall, while in Mozambique it caused deadly flooding and further contributed to widespread flooding in several countries.

Time_Annotation: A tropical disturbance developed within the ITCZ on February 19 southeast of Diego Garcia. On February 21, the MFR upgraded the system to Moderate Tropical Storm Gamede, and by February 23 it had reached tropical cyclone intensity. The cyclone passed west of Réunion on February 27, and on March 2 the MFR reclassified Gamede as an extratropical cyclone and tracked it for four more days.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The outer rainbands began affecting the Mascarene Islands (notably Mauritius and Réunion) on February 24. Later, the cyclone’s impact on Mauritius (where wind gusts reached 158 km/h and it caused fatalities), on neighboring Réunion with significant damage, on Madagascar along its east coast, and in the South African province of KwaZulu-Natal (with high waves affecting beaches and the port) identify the affected areas.
Main_Event_Annotation: The article notes that on February 21 the system was upgraded to Moderate Tropical Storm Gamede and by February 23 it had attained tropical cyclone intensity, supporting its classification as a Tropical Storm/Cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: Multiple sentences describe hazardous conditions: wind gusts were recorded (165 km/h, 195 km/h, 158 km/h, and 205 km/h) and heavy rainfall led to flooding that wrecked crops, damaged infrastructure, and washed out bridges.

Time_Annotation: An area of convection persisted southeast of the Chagos on March 26. On April 8, the MFR stopped tracking the system.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: Jaya again weakened as it approached eastern Madagascar and moved ashore about 25 km south of Sambava. It dropped heavy rainfall in the eastern portion of the country, resulting in significant flooding in the Sofia and Diana regions.
Main_Event_Annotation: A day after formation, the system intensified into Moderate Tropical Storm Jaya and then attained tropical cyclone status early on March 31, making it the sixth intense tropical cyclone of the season.
Hazards_Annotation: Jaya produced peak winds of 185 km/h (with gusts up to 125 km/h at Sambava and Antalaha) and heavy rainfall (a 24‑hour total of 216.1 mm at Toamasina), which resulted in significant flooding.

Time_Annotation: Early on February 12, PAGASA reported that a low-pressure area located about 140 km (87 mi) to the east of Surigao City in the Philippines had intensified into a tropical depression. Early the next morning, after the depression made landfall on Dinagat Island, PAGASA released its final advisory. Late on February 13, the remnants of Bising brought scattered rain showers across Southern Luzon, Bicol Region, and Visayas.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The text specifies the low‐pressure area was east of Surigao City in the Philippines and mentions locations such as Dinagat Island, Cebu, and affected regions (Southern Luzon, Bicol Region, Visayas), thereby indicating the Philippines as the affected country.
Main_Event_Annotation: The article describes the system as a tropical depression that intensified and made landfall – characteristics that align with the Tropical Storm/Cyclone category in the provided hazard table.
Hazards_Annotation: The event had peak windspeeds estimated at 45 km/h (indicative of a wind hazard) and produced scattered rain showers that led to mudslides on Cebu Island (a flood-related hazard).

Time_Annotation: The overall system developed a distinct low-pressure area on October 27; on October 29 the IMD designated it as Depression ARB 02; at 03:00 UTC on November 1 it was upgraded to a deep depression and 24 hours later to Cyclonic Storm Keila; it made landfall near Salalah, Oman around 18:00 UTC on November 2; and it dissipated on November 4 according to the IMD and on November 5 according to JTWC post-season analysis.

Time_Annotation: The article states: 'Pabuk originated in a low pressure area which formed in the South China Sea on December 28, which later became a depression on December 31. On January 1 at 06:00 UTC, it became a tropical storm with JMA naming it "Pabuk". It maintained its intensity until making landfall over the Pak Phanang District of Thailand on January 4 at 05:40 UTC. On the morning of January 5, it entered the basin, and the India Meteorological Department (IMD) began giving advisories to the system. Pabuk became a deep depression at 06:00 UTC the next day, and was further downgraded to a depression at 00:00 UTC on January 7. The next day, it weakened into a well-marked low pressure area.'
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The text mentions: 'Pabuk caused gusty winds and heavy rainfall over the Andaman and Nicobar Islands with no significant damage reported in the island. Time_Annotation: Yagi originated from a low-pressure area that formed on August 30, approximately 540 km (330 mi) northwest of Palau. On September 1, the system was classified as a tropical storm and named Yagi by the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA). It was last noted on September 9 as it moved southwestwards inland.
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The typhoon made landfall over Casiguran, Aurora in the Philippines, over Haiphong and Quảng Ninh in Vietnam, and near Wenchang in China's Hainan Province. Its remnants also caused catastrophic flooding and landslides in Myanmar, Laos, and Thailand.
Main_Event_Annotation: Vietnam Typhoon Yagi was described as a deadly and extremely destructive tropical cyclone and was classified as a tropical storm by the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA).
Hazards_Annotation: The storm reached Category 5-equivalent intensity with extreme wind speeds while the combination of Typhoon Yagi and the southwest monsoon led to heavy rains and widespread flash floods.

Time_Annotation: On November 24 an area of low pressure formed over land in Sri Lanka.[1] Early on November 26, the India Meteorological Department upgraded the deep depression to a Cyclonic Storm and named it Nisha. Early the next day the IMD reported that Cyclonic Storm Nisha had made landfall in Tamil Nadu, India, at 0030 UTC.[8] The IMD then reported that Nisha had weakened into a Depression and issued their last advisory the following day.[11][12]
Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The event originated over land in Sri Lanka as mentioned in 'On November 24 an area of low pressure formed over land in Sri Lanka.[1]' and later impacted India as indicated in 'Early the next day the IMD reported that Cyclonic Storm Nisha had made landfall in Tamil Nadu, India, at 0030 UTC.[8]'
Main_Event_Annotation: The event was designated a Cyclonic Storm when the IMD upgraded the system on November 26, as noted in 'Early on November 26, the India Meteorological Department upgraded the deep depression to a Cyclonic Storm and named it Nisha.' Additionally, the JTWC upgraded the system to Tropical Cyclone 06B, confirming its tropical cyclone status.
Hazards_Annotation: Hazard information is derived from the reported wind speeds. Specifically, 'Later that day the JTWC upgraded the Deep Depression to Tropical Cyclone 06B and reported that the depression had wind speeds equivalent to a tropical storm,[6]' and 'both the JTWC and the IMD reported that Nisha had reached its peak wind speeds of 55 kts (63 mph) and 45 knots (52 mph) respectively.[7]' indicate that wind is the primary hazard.

Main_Event_Annotation: The system was tracked and declared as a tropical depression by the Japan Meteorological Agency, PAGASA (which assigned the name Tonyo), and the Joint Typhoon Warning Center, indicating its classification as a tropical cyclone event.
Hazards_Annotation: The storm produced heavy rainfall (over 250 mm, with a peak of 858 mm) indicative of flood hazards and caused gusty winds that uprooted trees and ripped roofs, demonstrating wind hazards.
